summaries.example: Imagine a path drawn on a map that suddenly stops, even though there seems to be room to keep drawing. A spacetime singularity is somewhat like that, except the map represents space and time. Near a black hole, gravity can become so strong that paths for objects or light cannot continue in the usual way.
summaries.summary: A spacetime singularity is a place, or more carefully a situation, where the usual description of space and time breaks down. Scientists often describe this with an incomplete path: an object or observer could experience only a limited amount of time before the path cannot continue. Other ideas describe singularities as missing points or as extreme problems in spacetime’s curvature, but none is accepted in every case. General relativity predicts singularities in situations such as the beginning of the universe and the centers of many black holes. A black hole is a region whose gravity prevents anything from escaping once it crosses the event horizon. The entry explains why these ideas are difficult: a singularity may not be an ordinary object with a location, and different mathematical descriptions can highlight different problems. Scientists and philosophers also ask whether singularities are real parts of nature or signs that general relativity needs to be replaced by a deeper theory. Black holes connect these questions with thermodynamics and quantum theory, because they can be described as having temperature and entropy when quantum effects are considered.
key_ideas: General relativity allows singularities, but scientists do not agree on one perfect definition of them.
One important idea is that a singularity involves a path that ends too soon.
Some people think singularities show that general relativity stops working in extreme situations.
Others think singularities may be real features of the universe that we need to understand.
Black holes and singularities are connected, but a black hole also has its own puzzles about observation, time, and physics.
summaries.why_it_matters: Singularities help us ask where our best ideas about space, time, gravity, and physical laws work—and where they may stop working. Studying them also connects astronomy with big philosophical questions about what exists, what scientists can know, and whether a theory’s predictions describe reality or reveal its limits.

important_terms.definition: A breakdown in spacetime’s geometry or another basic part of the physical description of space and time.
A path through space and time that cannot be continued after a limited amount of time.
A region from which nothing, not even light, can escape.
The boundary around a black hole marking the point of no return.
The bending or stretching of spacetime associated with gravity.

questions_to_think_about: If a path stops, does that prove there is a hole, or could the map simply be incomplete?
Should a singularity be treated as a real thing or as a warning that a theory has reached its limits?
Why might different observers describe what happens near a black hole differently?
Can a mathematical model tell us what really exists in the universe?

summaries.example: Consider a collapsing star. Once its matter passes within a critical size, general relativity predicts an event horizon: a global boundary from which no light signal can reach the distant universe. Inside, future-directed paths may be incomplete, ending after only a finite amount of proper time. This does not automatically identify a missing point inside spacetime; it illustrates why path incompleteness and boundary localization are different proposals.
summaries.summary: The entry examines what singularities could be in relativistic spacetime and what their existence would mean. General relativity permits them, and singularity theorems show that they arise under conditions regarded as physically reasonable. Yet defining them precisely is difficult. The most common approach characterizes a singular spacetime by an incomplete, inextendible path of finite generalized affine length. This captures the idea that an observer or particle can reach an endpoint of its history without the path being extendible, but the physical meaning of generalized affine length is not transparent. Requiring geodesic incompleteness is too restrictive, while simply allowing any finite proper-time path counts harmless examples as singular. A second approach adds boundary points to represent locations missing from spacetime. This can work in simple mathematical examples, but black-hole and cosmological cases do not generally supply a unique place for such points, and proposed boundaries may have unacceptable separation properties. Curvature pathology offers another intuitive guide: tidal forces may become unbounded near a singularity. However, whether an observer experiences such pathology can depend on the observer’s motion, so curvature pathology is not a property of a region in a simple, observer-independent sense. These difficulties motivate disagreement over whether singularities are genuine physical structures or marks of general relativity’s limited domain. Black holes intensify the issue. Their event horizons are global causal boundaries, while quasi-local horizons attempt to identify black-hole behavior using nearby measurements. key_ideas: There is no universally accepted strict definition of singularity. Path incompleteness is the usual working criterion, but it has conceptual and physical limitations.

Boundary constructions try to represent a singularity as missing spacetime points. They face problems because incomplete paths do not always identify a unique location, and proposed boundaries can have pathological properties.
Curvature pathology, such as unbounded tidal forces, is neither necessary nor sufficient for every case of path incompleteness.
General relativity’s singularity theorems show that under certain physically motivated conditions, singular behavior cannot be avoided in important situations.
A black hole’s standard definition is global, while quasi-local definitions use nearby geometric behavior; these definitions need not serve the same purposes.
Singularities raise questions about determinism, the limits of general relativity, and whether quantum gravity will remove or reinterpret them.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic is a case study in how physics and philosophy interact. Mathematical definitions, physical interpretation, observation, and metaphysical assumptions all affect what scientists mean by a theoretical entity. Singularities also sit at the meeting point of general relativity, quantum theory, and thermodynamics, making them central to attempts to understand whether spacetime itself has deeper structure.

important_terms.definition: A failure in spacetime geometry or another fundamental physical structure, often characterized by an incomplete path.
A curve that cannot be extended further even though its relevant length, such as proper time, remains finite.
A spacetime that cannot be treated as a proper part of a larger spacetime of the relevant kind.
Time measured by a clock moving along a timelike worldline.
A boundary of a black-hole region defined globally by whether light can escape to the external universe.
A physical effect caused by differences in gravitational strength across neighboring locations.
The conjecture that physically realistic singularities are generally hidden behind event horizons.
The property that the later state of a quantum system is fixed by its earlier state through reversible, information-preserving evolution.

questions_to_think_about: Does a finite-length inextendible path describe a physical failure, or only a defect in a chosen mathematical model?
Why might incomplete paths fail to determine a unique missing point?
Should a theory’s prediction of singularities count as evidence that the theory is successful, unsuccessful, or both?
How does the global character of an event horizon affect what can count as an observation?
If quantum theory preserves information but black-hole evaporation appears not to, which assumptions should be revised?

summaries.example: Think about a video game world with a character following a road. If the road ends after ten minutes even though the game says the world is complete, players may wonder whether the road reaches a hidden hole or whether the game’s rules have failed. In spacetime, an incomplete path raises a similar question. But unlike a game map, spacetime may not sit inside a larger space where we can simply point to the missing place.
summaries.summary: This entry explores singularities as both a physics problem and a philosophical problem. In general relativity, a singularity signals that some basic part of the spacetime description has broken down. The disagreement begins when we ask how to define that breakdown. The leading idea uses path incompleteness: a possible worldline for an object or observer cannot be continued even though only a finite amount of proper time has passed. Yet not every short path indicates a serious physical problem. Some paths in ordinary, nonsingular spacetime can end because of extreme acceleration, while some geometrically well-behaved paths can still seem physically troubling. A common definition therefore uses a technically more general measure of path length, but its physical meaning remains unclear. Another proposal treats singularities as missing points and tries to attach a boundary to spacetime. This works easily for a flat sheet with a region removed, but it is much harder for a black hole or the beginning of the universe. In those cases, incomplete paths may not point to one shared location, and constructed boundaries can behave strangely. Curvature provides a different clue. Tidal forces may grow without limit, but their behavior can depend on the motion of the observer measuring them. Thus curvature pathology does not neatly define a singular region by itself. The entry presents a live disagreement: singularities may be genuine features predicted by general relativity, or they may show that the theory cannot describe extreme conditions. Black holes connect the debate to event horizons, determinism, and quantum gravity. key_ideas: Scientists agree that general relativity permits singularities, but they disagree about exactly what a singularity is.
The main definitions focus on paths that end too soon, points that seem to be missing, or extreme behavior in curvature.
Making a larger spacetime model can remove some artificial incomplete paths, which is why maximality is often required.
Adding boundary points sounds helpful, but in black-hole and Big Bang models there may be no clear location to add.
Some physicists see singularities as real possibilities; others see them as signs that general relativity is being used beyond its proper range.
Black holes make the issue important because their central singularities, horizons, thermodynamic behavior, and possible quantum effects are closely connected.
summaries.why_it_matters: The question of singularities tests how scientific theories work. It asks whether mathematical structures should be treated as real, how evidence can support claims about unobservable regions, and whether a theory’s failure is a discovery about nature or a signal to search for a better theory. These issues also help explain why black holes are important in modern physics.

important_terms.definition: A breakdown in spacetime’s geometry or another basic physical structure.
A route through space and time that ends after a finite amount of experienced time and cannot be extended.
The idea that a singularity is represented by points missing from the spacetime model.
The bending of spacetime that appears physically as gravity; extreme curvature can produce strong tidal effects.
The surface of a black hole beyond which light cannot escape to the outside universe.
A singularity visible from outside a black hole rather than hidden behind its horizon.
The ability of physical laws and starting information to determine later events.
A proposed deeper theory combining quantum physics with general relativity.

questions_to_think_about: When a mathematical path ends, what extra reason is needed to call the spacetime physically singular?
Could several definitions of singularity each be useful for different scientific questions?
Why might a boundary point be more than a convenient mathematical label?
Would a theory that predicts its own breakdown be a bad theory, or a useful guide to a better one?
What could happen to predictability if a naked singularity were visible from the rest of the universe?
